doc.title: Jimmy Cobb — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Growing up and learning drums in Washington
title: Howard Swing Masters and Armstrong alumni on the road
summary: Brower asks about the Howard Swing Masters; Cobb talks about Bill Hughes and Eddie Jones, each of whom spent a career with one band.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Where was the locus of that activity? Was that 7th and T?
Were they both in the Howard Swing Masters at that point? Were you aware of that thing going on?
I’m not sure about that. They may have been. I can’t put my finger on when exactly that was, the Howard Swing Masters. What do you mean, the house band at the Howard?
No. There was a band at Howard University called the Swing Masters, not officially a part of the university, but Bill Hughes talks about it. Benny talks about it.
That could have been, because Bill Hughes was in the marching band with us too. So that’s why . . .

Yeah. That’s where I know him from. Bill Hughes probably ain’t had but one gig in his life. He was like Harry Carney with Duke Ellington. One gig, all your life, like Harry Carney. Duke went to his mother and says, “I want to take your son on the road.” She said, “Okay, if you take care of him.” So Harry Carney wound up being Duke’s chauffeur and all that. I think he only had one gig his whole life, and that was with Duke Ellington’s band. Bill Hughes was like that too. He only had one gig. It was with Count Basie. Now he wound up – he’s the head of it or something, isn’t he?
So that was his thing. The bass player, Jones, his aspiration . . .
Eddie Jones’s aspiration all his life was to play with the Count Basie band. He got to do that. So, life fulfilled, I guess.
